BLM Tres Rios Field Office: Dawson project area UAS data George Woolsey 04 September, 2026 Section 1 Introduction The Dawson vegetation treatment project area is located near Dolores, Colorado (USA) on land managed by the BLM Southwest District, Tres Rios Field Office (TRFO). On April 29th and 30th, 2025, BLM Remote Sensing staff mapped approximately 2,000 acres of the Dawson site using an Uncrewed Aerial System (UAS). In total 24 flights were conducted to collect ~5,500 stereo-images. The raw imagery was then processed photogrammetrically with Agisoft Metashape software to produce high-resolution geospatial data products including 3D point cloud data and an RGB spectral orthomosaic. 1.1 Objective The objective of this analysis is to process the aerial point cloud data using the cloud2trees framework (Woolsey et al. 2025) for generating individual tree forest inventory data. cloud2trees provides a streamlined, open-source framework for generating broad-area individual tree inventories from aerial point cloud data. The primary outputs are spatial datasets of tree locations and crown polygons attributed with biophysical metrics such as height, crown dimensions, crown base height (CBH), diameter at breast height (DBH), and crown biomass. While height and location are inherently determined through the detection process, the framework augments these inventories with tree-level biophysical information determined via allometric estimates and integrated supplementary data. These high-resolution datasets support a wide range of applications including fire behavior modeling, evaluation of forest management activities, and habitat characterization.

Section 2 Point Cloud Processing In this section we’ll process the raw point cloud data using cloud2trees developed to provide accessible routines for processing point cloud data collected by airborne lidar or generated using UAS imagery and photogrammetry (e.g. structure from motion). The cloud2trees package can be installed by following the directions listed in the README file on GitHub. If one is still experiencing difficulties installing the package, see the example.R file which details how to install the package using a virgin R instance. ### ```{r,eval=T ## remotes helps us get packages hosted on github install.packages("remotes") ## get cloud2trees remotes::install_github(repo = "georgewoolsey/cloud2trees", upgrade = F) Load the standard libraries we use to do work # bread-and-butter library(tidyverse) # the tidyverse library(viridis) # viridis colors library(harrypotter) # hp colors library(RColorBrewer) # brewer colors library(scales) # work with number and plot scales library(latex2exp) # visualization library(mapview) # interactive html maps library(kableExtra) # tables library(patchwork) # combine plots library(ggnewscale) # ggnewscale library(cowplot) # cowplot # spatial analysis library(terra) # raster library(sf) # simple features library(lidR) # lidar data library(cloud2trees) # the cloud2trees 2.1 Data Location Let’s check out the location of the data we got # directory with the downloaded .las|.laz files f <- "d:/BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment/Final/PointCloud/Tiles" # f <- "d:/BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment/Final/PointCloud/Full/" # is there data? list.files(f, pattern = ".*\\.(laz|las)$") %>% length() ## [1] 187 # what files are in here? list.files(f, pattern = ".*\\.(laz|las)$")[1:3] ## [1] "BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment_PointCloud_202504-0-0.laz" ## [2] "BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment_PointCloud_202504-0-1.laz" ## [3] "BLM_CO_SWDF_DawsonFuelsTreatment_PointCloud_202504-0-10.laz" what information does lidR read from the catalog? ctg_temp <- lidR::readLAScatalog(f) ctg_temp ## class : LAScatalog (v1.2 format 2) ## extent : -20768836, 22184836, -17283836, 25668836 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax) ## coord. ref. : NAD83(2011) / UTM zone 12N ## area : 57184906611 km² ## points : 5.24 billion points ## type : airborne ## density : 0 points/m² ## num. files : 187 that’s a lot of points…can an ordinary laptop handle it? we’ll find out. We’ll set the options in the function to generate a CHM which represents a DSM with the ground removed and no other filtering. This high resolution (i.e. fine-grain) CHM will serve as the foundation for tree detection and slash pile detection as we can manipulate it to optimize the processing for both methods. # outdir c2t_output_dir <- "../data" c2t_process_dir <- file.path(c2t_output_dir, "point_cloud_processing_delivery") c2t_tracking_fnm <- file.path(c2t_process_dir, "processed_tracking_data.csv") ############################################################## # cloud2trees::cloud2raster ############################################################## if( !file.exists( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "chm_0.1m.tif") ) || !file.exists( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "dtm_0.25m.tif") ) ){ # time it st_temp <- Sys.time() # run it # cloud2trees cloud2raster_ans <- cloud2trees::cloud2raster( output_dir = c2t_output_dir , input_las_dir = f , accuracy_level = 2 , keep_intrmdt = T , dtm_res_m = 0.25 , chm_res_m = 0.1 , min_height = 0 # effectively generates a DSM based on non-ground points ) # timer mins_temp <- difftime(Sys.time(),st_temp,units = "mins") %>% as.numeric() # save tracking dplyr::tibble( timer_cloud2raster_mins = mins_temp ) %>% write.csv( file = c2t_tracking_fnm , row.names = F, append = F ) }else{ dtm_temp <- terra::rast( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "dtm_0.25m.tif") ) chm_temp <- terra::rast( file.path(c2t_process_dir, "chm_0.1m.tif") ) cloud2raster_ans <- list( "dtm_rast" = dtm_temp , "chm_rast" = chm_temp ) } let’s see what we got from cloud2trees::cloud2raster() cloud2raster_ans %>% names() ## [1] "dtm_rast" "chm_rast" there’s a DTM # plot to check out the fine-resolution DTM raster cloud2raster_ans$dtm_rast %>% terra::plot(col = harrypotter::hp(n=100, option = "mischief"), main = "DTM (m)") there’s a CHM # plot to check out the fine-resolution CHM raster cloud2raster_ans$chm_rast %>% terra::plot(col = viridis::plasma(n=100), main = "CHM (m)") let’s see some details about the CHM # what chm? The local maximum filter algorithm allows for a constant window size or a variable window size defined by a function. See the lidR package book section by point cloud processing expert Jean-Romain Roussel for excellent detail on ITD and defining window size. The itd_tuning() function is used to visually assess tree crown delineation results from different window size functions used for the detection of individual trees. itd_tuning() allows users to test different window size functions on a sample of data to determine which function is most suitable for the area being analyzed. The preferred function can then be used in the ws parameter in raster2trees() and cloud2trees(). Section 4 UAS Measurement Accuracy Evaluation In this section, we’ll mask the point cloud detected trees using the slash pile detections to get our final UAS point cloud-derived forest inventory tree list. Then we’ll bring in field-measured data to evaluate our tree detection accuracy. This accuracy evaluation will yield detection accuracy metric including precision, recall (i.e. detection rate), and F-score (overall accuracy or balanced accuracy). Precision is a measure of the proportion of trees that estimated by the UAS method that were actually trees. Recall is a measure of the proportion of field-measured trees that the UAS method correctly identified. The F-score balances precision and recall to create an overall accuracy measure. All of these metrics range between 0 and 1 with values close to one indicating higher tree detection accuracies. In open canopy ponderosa pine forests, tree detection rates generally range from 65-85% (Creasey et al. 2021; Swayze and Tinkham 2023; Tinkham and Woolsey 2024) with higher proportions of larger trees (e.g. 75-95%) being detected compared to smaller tree detection rates (55-75%). Field inventories carry well-documented challenges, including measurement error, subjective assessments, and data transcription errors (Elzinga et al. 2005; Westfall and Woodall 2007; Luoma et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2019; Sparks et al. 2024). This means that a comparison of the remote sensing forest measurement method against field data evaluates alignment with current operational practices rather than absolute environmental reality. Below is a list of notes (and unfortunately some weird things) about it. There are 65 rows (out of 1603) with any missing data. The missing parts are usually in a location-related column with several in a tree metric column. There are 43 DRC (diameter at root collar) observations with two separate values separated by a comma. There are 8 circumstances where there are potential duplicate trees - where plot, distance, and azimuth are identical, but tree information is different. In the metadata crown length is described as “length from first longest side of the adult tree canopy, in m” and crown width is described as “width from second longest side of the adult tree canopy, in m”. The plot column includes unit, treatment type, and plot ID whereas the tree_id column includes that information as well as a per-plot ID of each tree. The multiple DRC values are due to multiple stems splitting at ground level. I think we should treat these as one tree, as they’re recorded in the data. To combine the two stem values into a single DRC, we could either take the larger of the two or sum them. The location duplication issue is due to two trees (or more likely stems from the same individual that split below ground) growing very close together. We should continue to treat them as separate trees, as shown in the data. Height, cbh, length and width are all in meters. DRC is in cm. make a function that uses the following input data parameters to match predicted trees with validation/reference trees: pred_data: predicted data point locations as sf data ref_data: reference/validation/ground truth data point locations as sf data max_dist_m: radius of search for matching max_height_error_m: maximum allowable difference in height for to be considered correct match for work in ponderosa pine forests, we generally set the max_dist_m to a 3 m radius to account for tree lean and slight horizontal misalignment in GPS data collection with 3 m representing the crown radius of a mature tree. we also typically set the max_height_error_m to 2 m for ponderosa pine evaluation but will need to reduce here to account for shorter trees information used to inform the definition of “typical” crown width can be found in: Gill et al. 2000 Bechtold 2003 Bechtold 2004 Purves et al. 2007 Then, we’ll aggregate the instance matching results to evaluate omission rate (false negative rate or miss rate), commission rate (false positive rate), precision, recall (detection rate), and the F-score metric. As a reminder, true positive (TP) instances correctly match ground truth instances with a prediction, commission predictions do not match a ground truth instance (false positive; FP), and omissions are ground truth instances for which no predictions match (false negative; FN) \[\textrm{omission rate} = \frac{FN}{TP+FN}\] \[\textrm{commission rate} = \frac{FP}{TP+FP}\] \[\textrm{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP+FP}\] \[\textrm{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP+FN}\] \[ \textrm{F-score} = 2 \times \frac{\bigl(precision \times recall \bigr)}{\bigl(precision + recall \bigr)} \] ############################################################### ############################################################### ############################################################### ############################################################### # such as RMSE, MAPE, and Mean Error of individual tree form measurements (e.g. height, diameter) are calculated by aggregating the differences between the estimated tree attributes and the field reference values for instances classified as True Positives. These metrics tell us about the method’s ability to accurately quantify the form of the trees it successfully identified. to prepare our results for analysis, we will develop a function that aggregates the tree-level data into a single record for each metric-error measurement combination. this function will calculate detection performance metrics such as F-score, precision, and recall (using the confusion_matrix_scores_fn() we defined above), as well as individual tree physical measurement accuracy metrics including Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Error (ME), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) to assess the accuracy of our tree form measurements. this could be a valuable function for any future analysis comparing predictions to reference data. here are the individual tree physical measurement accuracy metric formulas: \[ \textrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_{i} - \hat{y_{i}})^{2}}{N}} \] \[ \textrm{ME} = \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\hat{y_{i}} - y_{i})}{N} \] \[ \textrm{MAPE} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left| \frac{y_{i} - \hat{y_{i}}}{y_{i}} \right| \] Where \(N\) is equal to the total number of correctly matched trees, \(y_i\) is the ground truth measured value and \(\hat{y_i}\) is the predicted value of \(i\) There is a lot going on in our agg_ground_truth_match() function but it’s application is straightforward enough: The minimum required input is a data frame of the raw instance matches with a column named match_grp which is string/factor with the levels “true positive”, “commission”, and “omission” as returned by the ground_truth_prediction_match() function Optionally, if the data contain columns with the prefix “diff_” the mean error (ME) is calculated for those columns with the return having the suffix “_mean” and the RMSE is calculated for those columns with the return having the suffix “_rmse” interpretation of the ME is enhanced if these “diff_” columns are calculated as the predicted value minus the actual value (e.g. pred_diameter_m - gt_diameter_m) Optionally, if the data contain columns with the prefix “pct_diff_” the mean absolute percent error (MAPE) is calculated for those columns with the return having the suffix “_mape” these “pct_diff_” columns are calculated as the actual value minus the predicted value divided by the actual value (e.g. (gt_diameter_m - pred_diameter_m)/gt_diameter_m) 4.5.1 Example: Physical measurement Accuracy we already demonstrated minimum use of the agg_ground_truth_match() function to get detection accuracy metrics, now we’ll accuracy metrics 4.7 Tree Detection Accuracy Results Here we’ll perform individual tree detection (ITD) performance evaluation of the UAS method to verify the it’s ability to segment individual trees. Our instance matching method pairs field-mapped trees to UAS-detected trees to calculate: Recall - the proportion of real field trees successfully detected by the UAS (or the inverse of omission errors) Precision - the proportion of UAS-detected trees that correspond to real trees (or the inverse of commission errors) F-score - the harmonic mean between recall and precsion representing balanced detection accuracy Combining individual-level tree detection metrics with plot-level canopy and height aggregates will establish the statistical confidence we need to scale the UAS spatial tree list data across the entire study area to evaluate treatment effects on residual spatial structure. This focus aligns with contemporary management in pinyon-juniper systems, which prioritizes horizontal canopy architecture, clump configuration, and treeless open gaps as ecologically meaningful indicators of ecosystem health and fuel-hazard risk across these arid landscapes. first, we’ll check out the overall, site-wide tree detection accuracy results agg_ground_truth_match_ans <- ground_truth_prediction_match_ans %>% sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% agg_ground_truth_match() %>% dplyr::bind_cols( ground_truth_prediction_match_ans %>% sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::summarise(plots_n = dplyr::n_distinct(plot)) ) %>% dplyr::relocate(plots_n) # Evaluating aggregated, plot-level forest inventory metrics helps us understand how accurately the UAS data captures broader forest structural metrics like canopy cover. Since the circular ground-based field plots are relatively small with a 10.0 m radius and 314.2 m² area, the plot-level field data is insufficient to directly quantify macro-spatial patterns like tree clump sizes and treeless opening gaps. Our objective is to use the complete-coverage UAS data to map these broad-scale spatial patterns across the entire study area. However, validating UAS-derived spatial patterns against small field plots introduces several scaling and alignment challenges. The constraints of small field plots amplify compounding measurement errors, including boundary edge effects that complicate whether a tree is “in” or “out” of the plot, minor GPS misalignments between ground-based positions and the UAS, and the notorious difficulty of measuring two-dimensional crown dimensions in the field. To overcome these fine-scale spatial discrepancies, we’ll focus our UAS evaluation on plot-level aggregate metrics that naturally smooth out localized spatial noise while still capturing the broad-scale forest structure required for our UAS validation objectives. We’ll use plot-level canopy cover as the primary horizontal metric because it directly captures canopy openness and tree cover without being heavily influenced by minor stem-mapping misalignments. To complement this horizontal dimension, we’ll evaluate mean tree height at the plot level to validate the vertical profile representation of the UAS data. We’ll calculate these plot-level metrics by aggregating tree-level UAS predictions and field-reference values irrespective of individual instance matching. Following the terminology established by Li (2009), plot tree height is defined as the average height of individual trees within a plot boundary. While Li (2009) used a diameter threshold of at least 5 inches DBH to calcuate plot tree height, we used a tree height threshold of 2 m applied to both the UAS and field trees. For both canopy cover and plot tree height, we’ll calculate Mean Error (ME) to quantify systematic over- or under-estimation (bias) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) to measure total prediction variance. We’ll assess UAS prediction accuracy at two spatial scales: Overall Study Site: Aggregating data across all field-measured plots to evaluate site-wide performance. Treatment Level: Aggregating data within the field-measured plots associated with each specific treatment, including the control units. Combining plot-level tree crown and height aggregations with individual-level tree detection metrics will establish the statistical confidence we need to scale the UAS spatial tree list data across the entire study area to evaluate treatment effects on residual spatial structure. This focus aligns with contemporary management paradigms in pinyon-juniper systems, which prioritize horizontal canopy architecture, clump configuration, and interspace connectivity as ecologically meaningful indicators of ecosystem health and fuel-hazard risk across arid landscapes. 4.9.1 Canopy Cover Evaluation We’ll start by evaluating UAS-predicted canopy cover compared to field-measured values. Recall that to obtain field-measured canopy cover, we averaged the field-recorded horizontal crown length and width to approximate a circular diameter, used that diameter to calculate a 2D circular crown area for each tree, and determined the proportion of each plot covered by these assumed circular crowns. For each plot, we’ll compare this proportion to the canopy cover predicted by the UAS using trees whose tree-top points fall within the plot boundaries irrespective of if a tree was matched as a true positive in our instance matching evaluation. Requiring the tree-top point to fall within the plot mimics the field technique of only measuring stems located inside the plot boundaries. The main caveats attached to this canopy cover accuracy evaluation are that measuring crown dimensions accurately using manual ground techniques is notoriously difficult, and the simple circular shape assumption rarely matches the irregular crown morphologies found in the real-world (Rautiainen et al. 2008; Gallardo-Salazar & Pompa-García 2020; Ren et al. 2024). # validation_plots_polygons %>% The UAS approach delineates crowns from an aerial perspective and utilizes a segmentation routine that prevents any two crowns from overlapping. Conversely, the field method assumes a perfectly circular crown extending symmetrically from the tree stem. In dense stands, this circular geometry causes field-calculated crowns to overlap in 2D space which may artificially reduce the total canopy cover. In reality, tree branches grow asymmetrically. For example, extending away from competitors to capture available sunlight. The UAS captures this irregular, outward branch expansion which may explain why it results in larger (and more realistic) canopy cover measurements than the field-based method. let’s check out a visual representation of that phenomenon by looking as some example plots after we define a plotting function # Other discrepancies include plot edge effects influencing which trees were determined to be “in” the plot, a few cases of undersegmentation by the UAS, standing dead trees not removed by the RGB spectral filter applied at the very beginning of this section, potential “missed” trees in the field plot data (or these trees were not included in the validation data due to not meeting the 2 m minimum tree height threshold or were removed due to other missing data like missing coordinates). Either way, the tendency of the UAS method to underpredict height at the upper-limit of plot tree height does not appear to be systematically due to a single factor.

Section 6 Tree Group Analysis Evaluate the spatial configuration of the detected trees focusing on horizontal heterogeneity and an investigation of tree clumps and openings. some relevant work includes: Spatial Patterns of Pinyon–Juniper Woodland Expansion in Central Nevada (Weisberg et al. 2007) Density-dependent tree mortality in pinyon-juniper woodlands (Greenwood and Weisberg 2008) Long-Term Effectiveness of Tree Removal to Re-Establish Sagebrush Steppe Vegetation and Associated Spatial Patterns in Surface Conditions and Soil Hydrologic Properties (Williams et al. 2020) 6.1 Group Tree Crowns While some research on tree spatial patterns use tree point locations buffered with a fixed radius (e.g. 3 m) to approximate the crown radius of a “typical” overstory tree (e.g. Churchill et al. (2016)), we’ll use the irregular, more realistic crown shapes identified from the aerial data to determine tree clump groups. Remember we are only looking at what could be considered “overstory” trees since we filtered the tree list to keep only trees that meet a certain minimum height threshold of 2 m treetops_sf %>% sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::select(tree_height_m) %>% summary() %>% knitr::kable(format = "markdown") tree_height_m Min. : 2.000 1st Qu.: 3.750 Median : 4.750 Mean : 4.757 3rd Qu.: 5.700 Max. :18.760 Since a primary objective of this analysis is to evaluate how different treatments influence forest structure, we’ll treat each unit as a discrete area and exclude any trees located outside of the unit boundaries from the clump classification process. This approach assumes that trees within a unit do not form functional clusters with those in adjacent areas (even though some units share a common border and we have data extending beyond the unit boundaries). This assumption prevents data from untreated control areas or differently treated areas from influencing the results when summarized by treatment type. This intentional ignorance of edge effects means that the scale of focus of this analysis is strictly on the treatment unit. define a function to make the tree clump groupings by treatment unit get_clumps_temp <- function(tree_list, buffer = 0) { # buffer and dissolve (arcGIS logic) clump_polys <- tree_list %>% dplyr::ungroup() %>% sf::st_buffer(buffer) %>% sf::st_union() %>% sf::st_cast("POLYGON") %>% sf::st_as_sf() %>% dplyr::mutate(clump_id = dplyr::row_number()) # attach to trees trees_with_clumps <- tree_list %>% # get rid of columns we'll create dplyr::select( -dplyr::any_of(c( "hey_xxxxxxxxxx" , "clump_id" , "clump_n_trees" , "clump_n_trees_grp" , "clump_dist_m" ))) %>% sf::st_join(clump_polys %>% dplyr::select(clump_id), join = sf::st_intersects, largest = T) %>% dplyr::group_by(clump_id) %>% dplyr::mutate( clump_n_trees = dplyr::n() , clump_n_trees_grp = dplyr::case_when( clump_n_trees == 1 ~ "Individual" , clump_n_trees >= 2 & clump_n_trees <= 4 ~ "2-4 trees" , clump_n_trees >= 5 & clump_n_trees <= 10 ~ "5-10 trees" , clump_n_trees > 10 ~ ">10 trees" # , clump_n_trees >= 5 & clump_n_trees <= 9 ~ "5-9 trees" # , clump_n_trees >= 10 & clump_n_trees <= 15 ~ "10-15 trees" # , clump_n_trees > 15 ~ ">15 trees" # # , T ~ "error" ) %>% factor( ordered = T , levels = c("Individual", "2-4 trees", "5-10 trees", ">10 trees") # , levels = c("Individual", "2-4 trees", "5-9 trees", "10-15 trees", ">15 trees") ) ) %>% dplyr::ungroup() # add back to clumps clump_polys <- clump_polys %>% dplyr::inner_join( trees_with_clumps %>% sf::st_drop_geometry() %>% dplyr::distinct(clump_id, clump_n_trees, clump_n_trees_grp) , by = "clump_id" ) return(list(clump_polys = clump_polys, tree_list = trees_with_clumps)) } # buffer for UAS-delineated crown polygons my_buffer <- 1 make the clump groups using the UAS-delineated crown polygons. because we are using the irregular crown shapes that align with real-world crowns and want to account for slight misalignment between the UAS GPS and on-the-ground conditions we’ll define clump group membership using a 0.5 m buffer on the crowns. Under this condition, trees that do not have interlocking crowns based on UAS delineations but are within 1 m of one another will be considered part of the same tree clump group. We’ll identify openings based on their distance from the nearest tree crown. We’ll use this same 1 m distance threshold in defining treeless openings, where each opening will be required to comprise continuous space at least 1 m away from the nearest tree. This 1 m buffer accounts for the zone of immediate canopy influence and ensures that areas categorized as open are functionally distinct from the canopy. This threshold is flexible and can be adjusted to meet specific management or analysis objectives (e.g. flame length; wildlife corridors). First, we’ll generate a distance raster where each cell represents the distance to the nearest tree clump group (i.e. crown) within the treatment unit boundary. Areas with a distance value of 1 m or greater are classified as openings and are defined by spatial connectedness, not a specific geometric shape. As such, they may be irregularly shaped as they are allowed to wind between clumps to follow a path where trees are distant. A single opening continues as long as the flow of open space is not entirely obstructed by surrounding tree groups. Once a gap is completely surrounded by canopy, the opening is closed off and is treated as a discrete spatial feature. # create function to pass a return from get_clump_summary() and get a distance raster get_clump_dist_rast_temp <- function(x, clump_dist_m = 3){ # For this specific project, the “uniform” thinning treatments provided explicit instructions for the spatial arrangement of post-treatment stand conditions: Uniform - Low Light intensity thinning: Leave 15 feet between tree crowns. 70% of the retained (i.e. leave) trees should be over 8 inches basal diameter if present and 30% should be between 2 inches and 8 inches in basal diameter. Uniform - High Heavy intensity thinning: Leave at least 30 feet between tree crowns; 70% of the retained (i.e. leave) trees should be over 8 inches basal diameter if present and 30% should be between 2 inches and 8 inches in basal diameter. The following is a subset of items provided in the general guidance for both “uniform” prescriptions that are most relevant for our evaluation: Cut all dead pinyon trees <8 inches in basal diameter. Leave all other standing dead trees for wildlife snags. Dead trees are not considered when applying the spacing guides above. Remove 70% of all woody shrubs (i.e. gambel oak and serviceberry); retain all gambel oak stems greater than 3 inches in basal diameter. All trees with green spray paint should be not be cut and piles should be placed at least 15 ft from the canopy of those trees. These have a small piece of equipment that are recording tree growth (Fig. 2). These point dendrometers are on the bole (main stem) of the tree, located 1-2 feet above the ground on the east side of the tree, and a shapefile of the trees approximate location has been provided. In addition to the above, the following apply: …. Except for leave trees, all live trees having a minimum size of one (1) inch basal diameter and a height of 12 inches shall be cut. Retain trees that contain raptor nests. No ponderosa pine trees should be cut Since we know our UAS-based individual tree delineation does not perfectly align with field-marked trees (66% F-score), we’ll combine UAS-delineated tree crowns that are spatially continuous (i.e. directly touching or overlapping) into singular “tree objects” for this evaluation of the treatment tree spacing compliance. We’ll then calculate the distance between spatially distinct post treatment tree objects for comparison against the prescription targets. Additionally, since the prescription requires that priority trees like ponderosa pine and wildlife trees are not removed, and thus excluded from the spacing guidelines, the average space between residual trees should be slightly lower than the targets (even if the spacing is perfectly implemented to prescription) due to these restrictions which require keeping more trees than would be needed to meet the spacing guidelines. As a reminder, we are only evaluating UAS-detected tree objects that have a minimum height of 2 m and have a top point that falls within a treatment unit boundary. This approach assumes that trees within a unit do not form functional clusters with those in adjacent areas (even though some units share a common border and we have data extending beyond the unit boundaries). This assumption prevents data from untreated control areas or differently treated areas from influencing the results when summarized by treatment type. This intentional ignorance of edge effects means that the scale of focus of this analysis is strictly on the treatment unit. A significant global result indicates that tree spacing changes with treatment type. library(lme4) # linear mixed-effects models # ?lme4::lmer() lm_nn_temp <- lme4::lmer( nearest_dist_m ~ trtmnt_type + trtmnt_unit_area_ha + (1 | trtmnt_block) , data = tree_obj_polys ) # summary(lm_nn_temp) here are the global results which indicate whether treatment type significantly influenced tree spacing after accounting for treatment unit size # Compute joint tests of the terms in a model # ?emmeans::joint_tests joint_tests_temp <- emmeans::joint_tests(lm_nn_temp) joint_tests_temp %>% knitr::kable(format = "markdown") model term df1 df2 F.ratio Chisq p.value trtmnt_type 3 Inf 1178.125 3534.375 0.0000000 trtmnt_unit_area_ha 1 Inf 0.339 0.339 0.5605054 the p-value for treatment type of 0.0000 indicates that the nearest-neighbor spacing differs significantly across the treatments after accounting for block variations and unit size 6.5.4 Pairwise Treatment Comparisons To identify which treatment(s) created unique tree spacing outcomes, we’ll perform post-hoc pairwise contrasts among the different treatment groups. determine if specific spacing targets were successfully met for the uniform treatments. Rather than comparing treatments to each other, this analysis evaluates each individual treatment’s estimated marginal mean (accounting for both unit size and block variation) against the prescription tree spacing target. The null hypothesis is that the true average tree spacing is less than or equal to the target.
